paragraphs.heading: Belief after the evidence
paragraphs.text: A posterior probability is what you get when you take a prior probability and update it with new information, using Bayes' rule. The new information is summed up in what is called the likelihood. The result is a conditional probability: a chance worked out given the evidence you now have. When still more information arrives, today's posterior can serve as the prior for another round of updating.

paragraphs.heading: The formal picture
paragraphs.text: In Bayesian statistics, the posterior describes how probable each value of the parameters θ is once the evidence X is known, and it is written p (θ | X). It is the reverse of the likelihood function, which gives the chance of the evidence given the parameters, p (X | θ). The posterior is proportional to the product Likelihood · Prior probability.

paragraphs.heading: Everything you know so far
paragraphs.text: Seen as a matter of knowledge, the posterior holds everything there is to know about an uncertain claim, such as a scientific hypothesis. That holds given what you knew beforehand and a mathematical model of the observations you have at that moment. In practice it usually describes how unsure we are about the values of some statistical parameters, given a set of observed data.

paragraphs.heading: Girls, boys and trousers
paragraphs.text: Imagine a school where 60% of students are boys and 40% are girls. Every boy wears trousers, while the girls wear trousers or skirts in equal numbers. From a distance you spot a random student and can only tell that they wear trousers. How likely is it that this is a girl? Before seeing anything, the chance of a girl is 0.4, and the chance that a girl wears trousers is 0.5. By the law of total probability, the chance that any student wears trousers is 0.8: half of the 0.4 who are girls, plus all of the 0.6 who are boys.

paragraphs.heading: Counting heads instead
paragraphs.text: A more intuitive route is to picture N students: 0.6N boys and 0.4N girls. The trouser wearers are all 0.6N boys plus half of the 0.4N girls, and the girls among them are that half of 0.4N. Work out the share and girls make up 25% of everyone in trousers. So the chance that the student you saw is a girl is 25%, and any Bayes-theorem problem can be worked through in this counting way.

paragraphs.heading: Summing it up in practice
paragraphs.text: From a posterior distribution you can draw single best guesses and ranges, such as the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate or the highest posterior density interval (HPDI). Although the idea is simple, the posterior usually cannot be worked out exactly, so it has to be approximated, either by analysis or by numerical methods. Because it depends on data that came out at random, the posterior is itself a random quantity. A common way to show how uncertain it is, is to give a credible interval.

paragraphs.heading: Posteriors in classification
paragraphs.text: When sorting observations into classes, posterior probabilities express how uncertain it is that an observation belongs to a given class. Statistical classification methods produce them by definition. Machine learning tools often give membership scores instead, which carry no probabilistic confidence. Converting such scores into class-membership probabilities is useful, because the probabilities can be compared and are easier to use in later steps.
